nameStory: The "three-seeded" part of this plant's name comes from its distinctive fruit capsules, which split open to reveal exactly three seeds inside. The "mercury" name is a bit puzzling - it was borrowed from an unrelated European plant that ancient herbalists associated with the Roman god Mercury, perhaps because both plants seemed to appear and disappear quickly in gardens.
description: Three-seeded Mercury is a small, weedy annual plant that most people walk right past without noticing. It grows 6-18 inches tall with a bushy, spreading habit and small, unremarkable greenish flowers that lack petals entirely. This humble member of the spurge family is one of those "little brown jobs" that botanists love to puzzle over, but it's actually quite distinctive once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to diamond-shaped leaves with toothed edges, arranged alternately along the stem. The leaves feel thin and somewhat papery when you rub them between your fingers, and they're usually 1-2 inches long with a slightly wrinkled texture.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish clusters tucked into the leaf joints - no colorful petals to catch your eye. Male and female flowers appear on the same plant, with the female flowers surrounded by a small, leaf-like bract that looks like a tiny ruffle.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, three-lobed capsules that feel bumpy to the touch and split open explosively when ripe, scattering exactly three mottled brown seeds. You might hear a faint popping sound on quiet days as the capsules burst open.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, bushy annual that forms spreading patches rather than growing straight up. The stems are often reddish-tinged and feel somewhat succulent when you squeeze them gently.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, often reddish stems that branch frequently and feel slightly sticky or waxy when touched. The stems are typically thicker at the base and taper toward the growing tips.

habitat: **[UNCERTAIN]** This species appears to prefer disturbed soils, waste areas, and edges of cultivated fields, much like its relatives in the three-seeded mercury group. Look for it in areas with rich, loose soil that gets occasional disturbance - think garden borders, vacant lots, and the edges of agricultural areas where the soil has been turned over.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their first oval leaves appearing bright green and tender. **[UNCERTAIN]** Seeds likely germinate when soil warms in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and begin flowering, though you'll need to look closely to spot the tiny green flower clusters. This is the best time for identification when both leaves and flowers are present.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and begin their explosive dispersal - listen for tiny popping sounds! Plants start to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants have died completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout next year. Look for dried stems and scattered seed capsules as evidence of last year's growth.

funFact: The seed capsules of three-seeded mercuries are like tiny botanical cannons - they can shoot their seeds up to 6 feet away when they explosively dehisce, using built-up tension in the capsule walls to launch the next generation into new territory!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with its close relatives Common Three-seeded Mercury and Virginia Three-seeded Mercury, but **[UNCERTAIN]** the specific distinguishing features of this particular species are not well-documented. All three-seeded mercuries share the same basic leaf shape, tiny green flowers, and three-seeded capsules, making field identification between species quite challenging.
contextualKnowledge: **[UNCERTAIN]** With only one recorded observation in New England, this species may be extremely rare in our region, possibly just a rare migrant or casual introduction. It's worth noting that three-seeded mercuries are notoriously difficult to distinguish from one another, and some botanists debate whether certain forms represent distinct species or just variations.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAIN]** Distinguishing this species from Common Three-seeded Mercury and other Acalypha species requires close examination of technical features like bract shape and seed surface patterns. The extremely low observation count suggests it may be distinguished by subtle habitat preferences or geographic range rather than obvious physical differences. If you think you've found this plant, careful documentation and expert verification would be valuable given its apparent rarity in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Three-seeded Mercury has more distinctly diamond-shaped leaves compared to its relatives like Virginia Three-seed Mercury, which tends to have more oval leaves.
Slender Three-seeded Mercury is distinguished from Common Three-seeded Mercury by its much thinner stems and narrower leaves, while Virginia Three-seed Mercury tends to be taller and more robust.

Virginia Three-seed Mercury differs from its close relative Slender Three-seed Mercury by having hairy, glandless bracts around its female flowers, while Slender Three-seed Mercury has sparsely hairy bracts dotted with tiny red glands.
